title: A lead and its interns: local models on one Mac

scenes.narration: This voice was generated on this Mac. [[ledger]] So was the first draft of these words, and the fact-check behind them. We'll come back to how. First, why that's worth doing.

Working with an AI coding assistant creates a steady stream of small jobs. [[deal]] Summarising a source file. Deciding if a pull request is housekeeping. Judging the sentiment of a review. Checking if a summary matches the code.

Hosted models bill every request by the token. [[one]] For one small job, that cost is negligible. [[volume]] But this repository triaged three hundred Scala pull requests against six questions each: one thousand eight hundred judgments. [[free]] On a local model, re-takes are free, so you iterate more.
Small jobs are also latency bound: the round trip can cost more than the work. [[local]] A local decision takes about a second, with no network and no rate limit.

And some text should never leave the machine. [[lock]] Unreleased code, private pull request descriptions, recordings of a person's voice. [[loopback]] The local gateway listens only on the machine itself.
The catch: [[catch]] local models are much smaller than hosted models, and they are sometimes confidently wrong.

So the question is not whether to use local or hosted models, but how to split the work between them. [[team]] Think of it as a team. [[lead]] Claude Opus five point five is the capable lead. [[interns]] The local models are interns on this Mac, each good at one junior job. [[plan]] We'll cover how they are reached, [[p2]] which jobs suit them, [[p3]] and how their work gets checked.

Part one: how the interns are reached. [[door]] One gateway on this Mac is the only door to the local models. [[clients]] Claude Code talks to it over MCP, the browser gets a chat site and an admin page, and anything that speaks the OpenAI API can use it too. [[in]] An intern comes in only when a request needs it, in about two seconds, [[out]] and goes home when it has been idle. [[desks]] They share twenty eight of the Mac's forty eight gigabytes, so when the desks are full, the one idle longest makes room.

Part two: which jobs suit the interns. [[sort]] Look at the jobs again. Most are choices rather than essays. [[jev]] A small local decision model called Jev-Style did this sorting. [[miss]] It got five of six jobs right.

A generating model writes an answer token by token, and the prose has to be parsed. [[pass]] A decision model scores every option in a closed list in a single forward pass, and returns probabilities. [[pr]] Here, a Scala pull request that updates a build plugin. [[answers]] Four questions, one pass: a dependency update, low risk, no release note needed, internal housekeeping. [[cost]] Fast, deterministic, and nothing to parse.

This repository triaged three hundred Scala pull requests with six yes or no questions. [[rank]] The ranking was good, but the default threshold flagged many pull requests that maintainers hadn't labelled. [[calib]] For the collections question, it flagged thirty nine, and nineteen were right.

Part three: how the interns' work gets checked. [[review]] A local model reviewed a short Python function and claimed it raised an IndexError. [[not]] It did not. [[nli]] A local fact-checking model agreed, with a probability of zero point seven two. [[real]] The real bug was that the last windows are partial, but still divided by n.

So generated work goes through checks a machine can verify: valid JSON, a pattern, a length, faithfulness to a source. [[retry]] Failures are fed back, and the intern tries again. [[lead]] If errors persist, the lead takes over.

The lead retains design, review and judgment. [[down]] Interns handle summaries, extraction, classification, boilerplate and first-pass triage, [[tools]] handed down through four tools: chat, decide, entail and iterate.

As promised: [[design]] this voice was designed from one sentence describing it. [[clone]] A local model saved and cloned that voice for every scene, so they all sound the same. [[words]] Whisper listened back and timed every word, which is how the animations know when to move.

Making this film was itself a stack of small jobs. [[interns]] The interns on this Mac drafted the narration, fact-checked it, voiced it and timed it. [[lead]] The lead wrote the storyboard and the animation code, and edited the script. [[same]] Same split, same reasons.
